segments.line: Here's the problem.
You've burned half your fuel in five days, mostly showing off. And there is no way to make more.
Gasoline comes from crude oil, heated and split apart in giant refineries. The Romans have nothing close.
Even strong alcohol, which some cars can burn, has to be distilled, and
Europe won't learn to distill alcohol for about another thousand years. That's real.
Mo has an idea.
Olive oil. Rome is drowning in olive oil. And here's the funny part. In
nineteen hundred, at the World's Fair in Paris, a diesel engine ran on peanut oil. That's real too.
So if your car were a diesel, olive oil might actually work. It isn't.
One cup in the tank, and
the engine coughs like it's dying. You
drain it by hand. It takes all night. Then
the tires. Roman soldiers wear sandals with iron nails in the soles, and they lose them everywhere.
Archaeologists still follow trails of those nails to find where Roman armies marched. That's real.
On day six, you find one. With your front tire. You
put on the spare. Now you have no spare. And
rubber doesn't exist here. The trees it comes from grow in South America, and nobody in Rome knows South America exists.
So the car is dying. Slowly. But even dying, it's the fastest thing in the world.
Rome's fastest messengers, changing horses at stations along the road, covered about
eighty kilometers a day. That's real.
Your car does that in under an hour. A
message from the edge of the empire in one day instead of a week. An
army that never gets tired. And
somebody very important is thinking the exact same thing.
